name: Celerix
description: Celerix is a SNT-compatible neurosynaptic accelerant that temporarily increases signal propagation velocity across motor and sensory neural pathways by upregulating myelin-analogue synthetic sheaths in the peripheral nervous system. The result is a measurable reduction in reaction time of 80-120 milliseconds — enough to matter significantly when facing augmented opponents. Helix designed it specifically to give unaugmented or lightly augmented users a competitive edge against chrome-heavy targets.
effects: Improved threat-tracking and predictive motor response
Smoother fine motor control under stress
Compatible with most standard BCI loadouts
side_effects: Incompatibility crashes with certain military-grade BCIs
Risk of synaptic fatigue — degraded reaction times post-use for 24-48 hours
Seizure risk in users with neural scar tissue
cultural_context: Celerix is the drug of choice for the technically minded runner who understands pharmacokinetics — people who talk about 'stacking windows' and 'optimal timing.' In Tier 3 combat circles it has an almost aspirational quality, associated with precision and skill rather than brute force. The neural_direct delivery means you need a BCI port, which prices out the lower Shelf. Knockoffs exist but the delivery mechanism is hard to replicate safely.
story_hooks: A street-level knockoff of Celerix is moving through the Shelf — it produces the reflex boost but causes catastrophic BCI port corrosion after three uses; someone is selling it knowingly
A runner discovers their Celerix prescription is being used by Helix as longitudinal neural data collection without consent — the drug is also a study
Two runners both dosed with Celerix face each other in a closed space; the fight comes down to who times their peak correctly
